text: A notebook is a wonderful place to explore and a terrible place to hide mistakes. The same notebook that took you an hour to write can take a colleague, or you next month, two hours to understand. Clean code here isn't about style points — it's about making your analysis something other people, including future you, can read, trust, and rerun.

Compare two versions of the same calculation on a tiny orders table. The messy version uses single-letter columns s, q, and p, and multiplies by the bare number 0.92 with no explanation. Nobody can tell what any of that means. Worse, it triggers pandas' SettingWithCopyWarning, because the result is a slice of the original DataFrame and we assign a new column straight into it.

The cleaned-up version uses full names like quantity and unit_price, turns 0.92 into a named constant called LOYALTY_DISCOUNT with a comment explaining why, and moves the logic into a function called add_order_total that copies its input before modifying it. Running it prints three completed rows with order totals of 18.4, 23.0, and 18.4 — same numbers, now something a reader can actually trust.

If you paste the same five lines into three cells, you have a function waiting to be written. A good notebook function does one job, takes its inputs as arguments, returns its result, and has a one-line docstring. Avoid functions that quietly read a global DataFrame defined in some earlier cell — that hidden dependency is exactly what breaks when cells run out of order.

Notebooks let you run cells in any order, and the kernel remembers everything. That's the source of the classic 'it worked yesterday' bug: a variable you deleted from the code still lives in memory. Build the habit of Kernel, then Restart & Run All, before you share anything. If it fails or produces different numbers, your notebook depends on state that isn't written down.

A layout that works for most analyses: title and purpose in a markdown cell, imports and settings in one cell at the top, load the raw data and do nothing else there, clean using functions, analyze with one idea per section, and conclusions in plain sentences with numbers. Keep comments for the why, not the what, and clear noisy outputs — printing a ten-thousand-row DataFrame helps no one.

To recap: use full, descriptive names and named constants instead of magic numbers, wrap repeated logic in small functions with docstrings that don't mutate their input, copy before you modify, and restart and run all before sharing. Next, we take the next step: moving that reusable logic out of the notebook entirely, into scripts and modules.
